title: Emrys and the Atlas
premise: In 1746, Orsen Blackwood, apprentice to a murdered mapmaker, is finishing the master's atlas of the occupied Highlands when an injured child is left at their door with a note: forget the face. The child carries proof that the official account of a village massacre is a fabrication, and the victors' historians are racing to seal the record. Orsen, who has spent a lifetime believing history happens elsewhere, must choose between invisibility and truth, hiding the child and the evidence inside the very atlas meant to preserve it. The book ends with Orsen testifying before a commission that wants them silenced, publishing the atlas under both names—the master's and their own—and taking the child in as family, knowing the record may cost them everything but refusing to let memory be redrawn.
about_author: I. M. Fairweather is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suppressed documents in provincial record offices before turning to fiction. They write about the people history almost forgot, and live quietly with two cats and an unhealthy attachment to old maps.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Coastline
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. In the mapmaker's shop, Orsen works alone on the late Master Aldous Vane's atlas, tracing coastlines he never lived to draw. Establishes Orsen's creed: maps are for other people's histories. Emotional beat: grief disguised as diligence, and the comfort of staying small and unseen.

chapters.title: A Knock After Curfew
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A child, roughly ten, collapses at the shop door carrying a satchel and a note reading 'forget the face.' Inside the satchel: a bloodstained journal naming officers responsible for the Glenmara massacre. Emotional beat: fear warring with the pull of conscience; Orsen nearly turns the child away.

chapters.title: What the Child Carried
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen examines the journal—Vane's handwriting interleaved with another's—and realizes the master was murdered for gathering testimony. The child, Sorcha, speaks little but draws the village from memory with unnerving precision. Emotional beat: dawning horror that the atlas itself may be evidence.

chapters.title: The Historian's Visit
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A courteous crown historian, Mr. Ellery Shaw, arrives to 'assist' with completing Vane's atlas—for the victors' version. He lingers over the unfinished Glenmara plate. Emotional beat: polite menace; Orsen performs ignorance while understanding the race has begun.

chapters.title: Learning to Be Quiet
chapters.summary: Sorcha's POV. Hidden in the shop's loft, Sorcha observes Orsen's routines and slowly stops flinching. Flashback fragments of Glenmara surface through drawings rather than words. Emotional beat: tentative trust; the first time Sorcha eats at a table instead of hiding.

chapters.title: The Master's Cipher
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Deciphering Vane's marginalia, Orsen finds the atlas plates encode witness testimonies in cartographic symbols—a coastline's curve spelling a name, a forest's density counting the dead. Emotional beat: awe and terror; the master planned this all along, and Orsen is his unwitting accomplice.

chapters.title: Debts and Denunciations
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A neighbor reports strangers asking about the shop. Orsen bribes a printer's devil for news: witnesses are disappearing before the commission arrives to take official statements. Emotional beat: isolation tightening; Orsen realizes silence is complicity now.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Kept Names
chapters.summary: Sorcha's POV. Orsen seeks out Mrs. Abernathy, a widow who once smuggled Vane's letters, and Sorcha secretly follows. She recognizes the child's surname and weeps. Emotional beat: found family's first outline; three strangers becoming a conspiracy of memory.

chapters.title: Shaw's Offer
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Shaw returns, offering Orsen royal patronage and protection if the atlas is completed 'accurately'—with Glenmara rendered as a loyalist victory. He mentions the child obliquely, testing. Emotional beat: temptation and revulsion; Orsen understands they are already suspected.

chapters.title: The Plate That Lies
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Under pressure, Orsen begins drawing the false Glenmara plate as cover while secretly engraving the true one beneath—a palimpsest visible only when held to light. Emotional beat: cold resolve; deception as craftsmanship, justice as forgery.

chapters.title: Sorcha Speaks
chapters.summary: Sorcha's POV. Sorcha finally tells what happened at Glenmara—not the massacre itself, but the aftermath: soldiers burning the records first, so no one could prove the village existed. Emotional beat: catharsis through speech; Orsen realizes the atlas isn't just evidence, it's resurrection.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Soldiers search the shop on a pretext of unpaid taxes. Orsen hides Sorcha inside the map chest, listening to boots overhead. They confiscate Vane's correspondence but miss the ciphered plates. Emotional beat: terror and luck; the net is closing.

chapters.title: Mrs. Abernathy's Arrest
chapters.summary: Sorcha's POV. News comes that Mrs. Abernathy has been taken for sedition. Sorcha blames herself; Orsen refuses to run, arguing flight abandons everyone Vane died for. Emotional beat: guilt fracturing the fragile household; love expressed as stubbornness.

chapters.title: The Printer's Bargain
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen approaches a disreputable printer willing to strike hidden copies of the true plate—for a price and total deniability. The arrangement is fragile, paid in Vane's silver. Emotional beat: desperate hope; justice outsourced to the underworld because the law serves the victors.

chapters.title: What Shaw Knows
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen tails Shaw and discovers he possesses Vane's confiscated letters—he knows about the cipher and is decoding it himself, not to expose the massacre but to bury it deeper. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into purpose; the enemy is patient and thorough.

chapters.title: The Commission Arrives
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The official inquiry opens in town, collecting sanitized testimony. Orsen petitions to appear as Vane's literary executor, requesting the atlas be entered into evidence. Emotional beat: trembling courage; stepping from the margins onto the record.

chapters.title: Testimony by Lamplight
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Before the commission, Orsen presents the atlas and, when challenged, holds the Glenmara plate to candlelight, revealing the palimpsest—the true village beneath the false one. Shaw objects smoothly; the panel wavers. Emotional beat: the climax's first blow; truth made physically undeniable.

chapters.title: The Witness in the Gallery
chapters.summary: Sorcha's POV. Against Orsen's instructions, Sorcha enters the hearing and identifies an officer present among the commissioners' guards. Chaos erupts; Sorcha is seized, and Orsen's petition is suspended. Emotional beat: sacrifice and fury; the child chooses memory over safety.

chapters.title: Ash and Ink
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Shaw offers one last deal: Sorcha's freedom for the plates and silence. Orsen refuses, and that night the shop burns—but the plates were moved hours earlier to the printer. Emotional beat: loss transfigured; everything burnable is gone, and the truth survives anyway.

chapters.title: The Atlas Goes Forth
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The hidden copies circulate through the printer's network while the official atlas publishes with the false plate—undercut within months by the palimpsest copies surfacing in Edinburgh and London. Shaw is quietly reassigned; the commission reopens. Emotional beat: vindication without triumph; the record bends toward truth.

chapters.title: Mrs. Abernathy Comes Home
chapters.summary: Sorcha's POV. Released after the inquiry shifts, Mrs. Abernathy returns, and the three form an odd household above the rebuilt shop. Sorcha begins formal schooling, her drawings pinned to the wall beside Vane's proofs. Emotional beat: healing; found family solidified into something permanent.

chapters.title: Both Names on the Cover
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Years later, Orsen publishes the completed atlas under both names—Aldous Vane and Orsen Blackwood—with a dedication page listing the dead of Glenmara. Sorcha, grown, adds the final survey plate herself. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; memory kept not by heroes but by those who refused to look away.
